guidance.title: Know your rights
guidance.intro: Plain-language summaries of rights that protect you in Sri Lanka. Choose a topic to read more.
guidance.reviewNotice: This information is general guidance, not legal advice. It must be reviewed by a qualified lawyer before it is treated as advice for a specific case.
guidance.notFound: That topic does not exist. Choose one from the list below.

arrest_detention.title: Rights during arrest and detention
arrest_detention.summary: What the police may and may not do if you are arrested or held.
points: If you are arrested, the police must tell you why you are being arrested.
You cannot be held without being produced before a magistrate. In most cases you must be brought before a magistrate within 24 hours of your arrest, not counting travel time.
You have the right to talk to a lawyer and to have a lawyer present. If you cannot afford one, you can ask for free legal aid.
You may inform a relative or a friend that you have been arrested and where you are being held.
The police must record your arrest. You, or a person on your behalf, can ask which station you are being held at.
You must be treated humanely. Torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment are prohibited and are crimes under Sri Lankan law.
Anything you say can be used in court, so it is sensible to speak to a lawyer before answering questions about the offence.

discrimination_harassment.title: Protection from discrimination and harassment
discrimination_harassment.summary: What you can do if you are treated unfairly or harassed because of who you are.
points: Every person is equal before the law. The Constitution forbids the state from discriminating against you on grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion or place of birth.
Discrimination by a state institution — for example refusing a service, a licence or a benefit because of who you are — can be challenged through fundamental rights applications.

Harassment, including sexual harassment at work or in public institutions, is a crime. You can complain to the police, and at work you can also complain to the head of your institution or a labour tribunal.
Keep records: dates, places, what was said or done, and the names of anyone who saw it. Written records make a complaint much stronger.
You do not need a lawyer to make a police complaint. A friend or family member can help you write it, and legal aid organisations can help you for free.

legal_aid.title: Free legal aid
legal_aid.summary: How to get a lawyer's help even if you cannot pay for one.
points: Free legal aid means advice and representation from a lawyer at no cost, for people who cannot afford to pay.
Legal aid is available for many kinds of problems: family matters, land disputes, employment problems, criminal defence and complaints about discrimination.
The Legal Aid Commission of Sri Lanka has offices across the country and can be reached by phone on 1951. Many NGOs also give free legal help — see the legal resource directory in this app.
When you go for legal aid, bring any documents about your problem: letters, agreements, receipts, medical or police records.
You may bring a trusted person with you. Asking for legal help does not create any record that identifies you in this app.

language.heading: Choose your language
language.body: Pick the language you are most comfortable reading. You can change it any time from the top of any screen.

privacy.heading: You stay anonymous
privacy.body: We never ask for your name, your phone number, or your email address.
privacy.body2: Instead you get a reference code. That code is the only way back to your case — and it is yours alone.

safety.heading: Leave instantly, any time
safety.body: If someone comes near, tap the exit button in the corner. The screen clears at once and nothing you typed is kept.
safety.body2: You can find it on every screen while you are reporting.
